short_text.text: In 1878 Eadweard Muybridge used a row of cameras to photograph a galloping horse, frame by frame. The photos showed details of motion that the eye can't catch. Futurist painters chased the same idea: show movement over time in one image.

In 1883 an Edison power station opened in central Milan, one of the first in Europe. Electric light changed what a city looked like at night. The Futurists loved it and painted it as a sign of the modern world.
In 1899 the car company FIAT was founded in Turin. Northern Italy was turning industrial, with factories, cars and fast-growing cities. That shift is the backdrop to Futurism.

In 1906 the Simplon railway tunnel opened under the Alps, linking Italy and Switzerland. Milan celebrated the same year with an international exhibition themed on transport. Trains and travel were the height of modern.

In 1907 the French philosopher Henri Bergson published 'Creative Evolution'. He argued that life is constant flow and change, not a row of fixed moments. Boccioni read Bergson, and that idea shows up in his paintings of motion and feeling.

Around 1907 and 1908, Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque began breaking objects into flat, angled pieces seen from several sides at once. This became known as Cubism. The Futurists borrowed the broken-up look but added what Cubism mostly left out: speed and motion.

On 20 February 1909 the Italian poet Filippo Tommaso Marinetti published the 'Founding Manifesto of Futurism' on the front page of the Paris newspaper Le Figaro. It praised speed, machines and everything new, and attacked museums and the past. It even claimed a roaring race car was more beautiful than the ancient Greek statue called the Victory of Samothrace.

title.text: Futurist painters write their own rules

short_text.text: In 1910 a group of painters including Boccioni, Carrà, Russolo, Balla and Severini signed manifestos about painting. The 'Technical Manifesto' from April 1910 said painters should show movement and the energy of modern life, not still poses. That's basically the rulebook for the paintings in this guide.

In February 1912 the Futurist painters showed their work at the Bernheim-Jeune gallery in Paris. The show then travelled to London and Berlin. It brought Italian Futurism to an international audience.

In March 1913 Luigi Russolo wrote 'The Art of Noises', a manifesto saying music should include the sounds of machines, traffic and factories. He then built noise-making instruments he called intonarumori, meaning 'noise intoners'. He's the same person who painted the car in this guide.

World War I broke out in July 1914. Italy stayed neutral at first, while the Futurists campaigned loudly for it to join. Italy entered the war in May 1915, and Boccioni, Russolo and Marinetti signed up with a volunteer battalion of cyclists and motorists.
In August 1916 Umberto Boccioni died near Verona after falling from a horse during military training. He was 33. His death cut short the career of one of Futurism's main painters and thinkers.
